source_text: Proxime tibi, dilectissima in domino conserva, quid foeminae sanctae, matrimonio quacunque sorte adempto, sectandum sit, ut potui prosecutus sum. Nunc ad secunda consilia convertamur, respectu humanae infirmitatis, quarumdam exemplis admonentibus, quae divortio vel mariti excessu, oblata continentiae occasione, non modo abjecerunt opportunitatem tanti boni, sed ne in nubendo quidem rursum disciplinae meminisse voluerunt, ut in Domino potissimum nuberent. Itaque mihi confusus est animus, ne qui nuper te ad univiratus et viduitatis perseverantiam hortatus sum, nunc mentione nuptiarum, proclivium tibi labendi ab altioribus faciam. Quod si integre sapis, certe scis id servandum tibi esse, quod sit utilius. Quod vero difficile est, et non sine necessitatibus et hoc maximum propositum vitae supremi praesidii. Nec mihi de isto quoque referendi ad te caussae fuissent, nisi graviorem meam sollicitudinem comprehendissem. Nam quanto grandis est continentia carnis, quae viduitatem ministrat, tanto, si non sustineatur, ignoscibilis videri potest; difficilium enim facilis est venia. Quanto autem nubere in Domino perpetrabile est, uti nostrae potestatis, tanto culpabilius est non observare quod possis. Eo accedit quod Apostolus de viduis quidem et innuptis, ut ita permaneant, suadet, cum dicit: Cupio autem omnes meo exemplo perseverare. De nubendo vero in Domino, cum dicit: tantum in Domino, jam non suadet, sed exserte jubet. Igitur in ista maxime specie, nisi obsequimur, periclitamur, quia suasum impune quid negligas, quam jussum, quod illud de consilio veniat et voluntati proponatur, hoc autem de potestate descendat et necessitati obligetur, illic libertas, hic contumacia delinquere videatur.
pass_a_gloss: Next to you, my dearest fellow-servant in the Lord, I have pursued as far as I could what a holy woman, from whom marriage has been taken away in any circumstance, ought to follow. Now we will turn to second thoughts, with regard to human weakness, examples of certain women warning us, who, having been offered the opportunity of continence either by divorce or by the death of a husband, not only rejected the opportunity of such a great good, but also did not want to remember the discipline even when marrying again, so that they might marry in the Lord especially. And so my mind is confused, lest I, who recently urged you to the perseverance of being a one-man woman and a widow, now, by mentioning marriage, make it easy for you to slip away from higher things. But if you are wise in an intact way, you certainly know that you ought to keep what is more useful for you. What is difficult, and not without necessities, is also this greatest proposal of the supreme aid of life. Nor would I have had to refer this matter to you, unless I had understood my own more serious concern. For as great as the continence of the flesh is, which serves widowhood, so, if it is not sustained, it can seem excusable; for what is difficult has an easy pardon. But as far as marrying in the Lord is possible for us, to the extent of our power, so it is more culpable not to observe what you can. This is added to the fact that the Apostle advises widows and unmarried women to remain as they are, when he says: I wish all to persevere according to my example. But concerning marrying in the Lord, when he says: only in the Lord, he no longer advises, but openly commands. Therefore, in this matter especially, if we do not obey, we are in danger, because to neglect what is advised is pardoned with impunity, whereas what is commanded descends from power and is obligated to necessity, there liberty seems to sin, here contumacy seems to sin.

pass_b_english: I have done my best to lay out what a holy woman ought to pursue once marriage has been taken from her, no matter the circumstances, my dearest fellow servant in the Lord. Now we must turn to second thoughts—concessions to human weakness—prompted by the example of certain women who, given the chance to live continent after divorce or a husband’s death, not only threw away so great a good but also refused to remember the discipline even when remarrying, so that they would marry in the Lord above all. That is why my mind is troubled: I who recently urged you to persevere as a one-man woman and a widow may now, by merely mentioning marriage, make it easier for you to slip down from higher things. But if you are truly wise, you know you must keep what is more useful for you. What is difficult, and not without hardships, is also this greatest proposal of the supreme aid of life. I would not have needed to bring this up at all unless I had grasped how serious my concern for you is. For the greater the continence of the flesh that serves widowhood, the more excusable its failure may seem; what is difficult finds easy pardon. But to the extent that marrying in the Lord lies within our power, it is all the more culpable not to observe what you can. This is reinforced by the fact that the Apostle merely advises widows and unmarried women to remain as they are when he says, ‘I wish all to persevere according to my example’ (1 Cor 7:40), whereas concerning marrying in the Lord, when he says ‘only in the Lord,’ he no longer advises but openly commands. Therefore, in this matter especially, if we do not obey we are in danger, because neglecting what is advised goes unpunished, but what is commanded issues from authority and binds necessity; there liberty seems to sin, here contumacy seems to sin.

review.notes: The translation accurately captures the nuances of the Latin text. Pass A and Pass B both correctly handle the complex conditional and causal structures. The scripture citation (1 Cor 7:40) added in Pass B is a correct identification of the quoted phrase 'Cupio autem omnes meo exemplo perseverare'.
